questions.title: Red face card from 52 cards
questions.text: A card is selected at random from a deck of 52 playing cards. The probability of it being a red face card is:
steps: ② Face cards: J, Q, K in each suit
questions.remember: 52 cards = 4 suits × 13. Face cards = J, Q, K (12 in all: 6 red, 6 black). Aces are NOT face cards.
questions.trap: Picking 3/13. That is ALL 12 face cards; only the red ones count.

questions.title: A spade or a king
questions.text: A card is drawn at random from a pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that the card drawn is a spade or a king?
steps: ② Kings: 4, but the king of spades is already counted
questions.remember: 'A or B': count A, add B, then subtract the cards that are BOTH.
questions.trap: Adding 13 + 4 = 17. The king of spades gets counted twice.
questions.tryit: One card from 52: P(a heart or a face card)?

questions.title: Winning is 0.21: probability of losing
questions.text: If the probability of a player winning a game is 0.21, then the probability of him losing the same game is:
steps: ① Win and lose are complementary
questions.remember: P(E) + P(not E) = 1. A probability is a number from 0 to 1, never more than 1.
questions.trap: Picking 0.79%. That means 0.0079, a tiny number.

questions.title: 6 cards missing: probability of a heart
questions.text: 2 cards of diamonds and 4 cards of spades are missing from a pack of 52 cards. A card is drawn at random from this pack. The probability of getting a card of heart is:
questions.remember: Cards removed? Recount BOTH: the total (bottom) and the favourable cards (top).
questions.trap: Keeping 52 at the bottom (13/52). The pack now has only 46 cards.
questions.tryit: From the same pack: P(a spade)?

questions.title: T-shirts 4 to 99: square or cube
questions.text: T-shirts marked with numbers 4 to 99 are placed in a box. Gunika is fond of numbers. She randomly takes out a T-shirt from this box. The probability that she gets a T-shirt marked with a number that is either a perfect square or a perfect cube is:
questions.remember:
Numbers from a to b: b − a + 1 of them.
'Square OR cube': subtract the numbers that are both (like 64).
questions.trap: Using 99 or 100 as the total. 4 to 99 is 96 numbers.
questions.tryit: A number from 1 to 50: P(perfect square)?

questions.title: Two dice: less than 4 on each die
questions.text: Two dice are rolled simultaneously. The probability of getting number less than 4 on each die is:
questions.remember: Two dice: 36 equally likely outcomes. 'On each die' ⟹ multiply the choices: 3 × 3.
questions.trap: Counting only (1,1), (2,2), (3,3). Different numbers on the two dice count too.
questions.tryit: Two dice: P(both show even numbers)?

questions.title: Assertion–Reason: multiples of 4 and two coins
questions.text:
Assertion (A): The probability that a number selected at random from the numbers 1, 2, 3, ..., 15 is a multiple of 4, is 1/3.
Reason (R): Two different coins are tossed simultaneously. The probability of getting at least one head is 3/4.
opts: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
steps: ② P = 3/15 = 1/5, not 1/3 ⟹ A is false  ✗
③ Two coins: HH, HT, TH, TT
④ At least one head: 3 of 4 ⟹ R is true  ✓
questions.remember: Assertion–Reason: check A and R separately first. Here they are about different experiments.
questions.trap: Thinking '3 numbers' means 1/3. It is 3 out of 15 = 1/5.
questions.tryit: Three coins are tossed: P(at least one head)?

questions.title: Two dice: difference of 2
questions.text: Two dice are thrown at the same time. Determine the probability that the difference of the numbers on the two dice is 2.
questions.remember: Two dice: draw the 6 × 6 grid. Equal differences sit on diagonals.
questions.trap: Counting (1,3) and (3,1) as one outcome. They are different outcomes.

questions.title: Two dice: multiples, and a perfect-square product
questions.text:
Two dice are rolled together. Find the probability of getting:
(i) a multiple of 2 on one and a multiple of 3 on the other die.
(ii) the product of two numbers on the top of the two dice is a perfect square number.
steps: ② Or the other way round: another 6
questions.remember: 'On one … on the other' ⟹ count both orders, then remove pairs counted twice.
questions.trap: (i): forgetting the reverse order, or counting (6, 6) twice (12/36).

questions.title: Face cards of spades removed
questions.text:
All face cards of spades are removed from a pack of 52 playing cards and the remaining pack is shuffled well. A card is then drawn at random from the remaining pack. Find the probability of getting:
(a) a face card
(b) an ace or a jack
steps: ① J, Q, K of spades removed ⟹ 52 − 3 = 49 cards
questions.remember: Cards removed: update the total AND each count. Ask: was any of THESE removed?
questions.trap: (b): counting 4 jacks. The jack of spades is gone, so only 3 remain.
